episodes.172006: Early in the morning of the third, an outflow reinforced cold front slipped southward into the region. This surface boundary stalled out across the South Plains and Rolling Plains during the daytime. Warm temperatures by early afternoon allowed convective temperatures to be breached and isolated thunderstorms developed across the central portions of the South Plains. A couple of these isolated thunderstorms produced severe wind gusts including an 84mph wind gust near Wolfforth (Lubbock County).
episodes.172393: During the afternoon and evening hours of September 3rd, a combination of a moist, unstable environment and relatively light steering level winds over the Ohio Valley facilitated the development of slow moving showers and thunderstorms which produced heavy rainfall across southern Indiana. Several broken lines of convection drifted from west to east across the region, spurred on by 1000-1500 J/kg MLCAPE and Precipitable Water values approaching 2 inches. A weak mid-level low across the mid-Mississippi Valley also contributed to broad uplift across the region, with precipitation being widespread across most of the lower Midwest and Ohio Valley during the afternoon of September 3rd. Where heavy thunderstorms lingered the longest, flash flooding was reported, with rainfall reports exceeding 10 inches in isolated areas. This heavy rainfall contributed to particularly severe flash flooding in Jefferson County, Indiana along Brushy Fork, where several homes were washed away and one fatality was reported.
episodes.172806: West Texas was on the western edge of an upper trough. Abundant moisture and lift were across the area. These conditions allowed for more rain to develop and move over already saturated soils which resulted in flash flooding.
episodes.172815: An upper level trough extended from the Mississippi River Valley southwest to Texas. Numerous boundaries were across West Texas from previous thunderstorms. High moisture and instability were also across the area. These conditions contributed to rain developing and moving over already saturated soils. This resulted in flash flooding across the Big Bend area of Texas.
episodes.173035: Lightning strike causes fire at apartment complex near High Point in Pinellas County.
episodes.173168: Slow moving showers and thunderstorms developed during the afternoon hours in a warm and humid airmass.
episodes.173169: Slow moving showers and thunderstorms developed during the afternoon hours in a warm and humid airmass.
episodes.173177: A band of thunderstorms containing rainfall rates up to two inches per hour trained over parts of southwest Indiana. The storms produced some urban flash flooding. The storms intensified during the heat of the day ahead of a 500 mb shortwave trough drifting eastward toward the Ohio River Valley. A tropical air mass was firmly entrenched, with precipitable water values well above the 90th percentile for early September. Effective vertical wind shear from 20 to 25 knots resulted in loosely organized bands of storms. The mean steering flow was parallel to the synoptic forcing, which caused training of the bands of storms with heavy rainfall.
episodes.173179: A band of thunderstorms containing rainfall rates up to two inches per hour trained over parts of northwest Kentucky. The storms produced some urban flash flooding. The storms intensified during the heat of the day ahead of a 500 mb shortwave trough drifting eastward toward the Ohio River Valley. A tropical air mass was firmly entrenched, with precipitable water values well above the 90th percentile for early September. Effective vertical wind shear from 20 to 25 knots resulted in loosely organized bands of storms. The mean steering flow was parallel to the synoptic forcing, which caused training of the bands of storms with heavy rainfall.
episodes.173249: Under a classic setup for storm motion from the Northern Arizona high terrain to Southern Arizona lower deserts, with the monsoon 500mb high positioned over Nevada and Utah, a few multicell storm clusters developed and progressed west-southwest through the lower deserts in the afternoon and evening hours of the 2nd. Increased east-northeast steering flow resulted in relatively high shear values for the monsoon (Sfc-6km shear around 25-30 kts) and very steep mid-level lapse rate (8-8.5 C/km) supported the organized multicellular storm mode with robust updrafts. Inversely, very high DCAPE values, up to 1500-1800 J/kg, supported very strong downbursts. Moisture levels were also above normal which, in combination with the strong updrafts, supported high rainfall rates (1.5-2 inches per hour average). There were a few multicell clusters that moved through Southern Arizona. One through the southeast parts of the greater Phoenix area, another that developed in Yavapai County before descending southwest along US-60 in Maricopa and La Paz Counties, and a third that developed off the Kofa Wilderness terrain south of Quartzsite before being caught by the cluster descending along US-60. Each cluster produced damaging winds, dense blowing dust, small to severe hail, and localized flash flooding.
episodes.173254: A mid-level trough moved over a moist conditionally unstable airmass. Thunderstorms developed along the seabreeze early in the day and moved inland to Lavaca County. Lightning from one of these storms started a fire at a storage tank battery. Later in the day a surface trough generated thunderstorms over the central part of the area. Some of these storms produced locally heavy rain that led to minor flooding.
episodes.173491: Showers and thunderstorms developed ahead of a slow moving upper level disturbance that tracked eastward across the southern Plains into the lower and middle Mississippi Valley from the 2nd to the early morning of the 3rd. Several reports of flash flooding were received south of Highway 60 from Aurora and Cassville, and eastward toward Ava. Rainfall accumulations for the 24-hour period ending at 1 AM on 9/3/22 showed a large area of one to two inches along and east of a line from Joplin to Versailles, with greater than two inches along and south of a line from Monett to Mountain Grove. A few locations in Douglas County received over 5 inches of rain.
episodes.173578: During the afternoon and evening hours on September 3rd, a combination of ample moisture and sufficient instability provided the necessary ingredients for widespread convection, resulting in locally heavy rainfall and isolated wind damage reports. On the synoptic scale, a weak mid-level disturbance was located across the mid-Mississippi Valley, with a surface low located across western Kentucky. Ahead of this disturbance, a moist air mass was located across central Kentucky, with Precipitable Water values approaching, and in some locations, exceeding 2 inches during the afternoon hours on the 3rd. SBCAPE in excess of 2000 J/kg was sufficient for widespread convection, and while lapse rates and DCAPE were not particularly suggestive of widespread damaging winds, isolated wind damage was observed with the strongest storms, located across Simpson and Warren County. While severe weather was not prevalent across north central Kentucky, multiple waves of heavy rainfall from relatively slow-moving showers and thunderstorms resulted in flash flooding, particularly across Trimble, Shelby, and Franklin County. Multiple reports of road closures and damage to homes along rivers and streams were reported in the aforementioned areas.
episodes.173676: A line of strong thunderstorms formed along an advancing cold front early in the morning on 9/3, eventually tracking into northern lower Michigan and producing heavy rainfall. Additional storms initiated just behind the line and continued to produce heavy rainfall in the vicinity of Little Traverse Bay, leading to significant erosion of the shoulder of M-119. A 24 hour rainfall total of 2.80 inches was measured 1 mile NNE of Harbor Springs at 9:30 AM EST with the majority of that falling in a 3 hour period that morning.
episodes.173677: A line of strong storms initiated along a cold front over northern Lake Michigan on the morning of 9/3, eventually tracking southeast and producing wind gusts in excess of 40 mph over the nearshore waters.
episodes.173678: A cluster of strong thunderstorms initiated over the far southeastern portion of the CWA, eventually moving over the Lake Huron nearshore waters and producing wind gusts in excess of 40 mph as the line tracked southeast.
episodes.174029: Deep monsoon moisture and light shear in the atmosphere brought strong to severe storms over northern Arizona with local flash flooding.
episodes.174123: A large storm system stretching from the mid-Mississippi Valley northward into the Great Lakes region on September 2nd through September 4, 2022, along with an abundant amount of moisture resulted in scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms across middle Tennessee. Due to slow storm motions and training of thunderstorms, heavy rain and areas of flash flooding were the primary threat during this event with impacts mainly felt near and south of Interstate 40. Several reports of flash flooding were received along with heavy rainfall totals of 3 to 6 inches.
episodes.174134: Isolated to scattered thunderstorms developed over portions of Northwest Kansas and extreme Southwest Nebraska, moving south. As the storms moved across Northwest Kansas, wind gusts up to 70 mph caused damage to a Cottonwood tree and small tents in eastern Graham County. As storms moved over eastern Wichita County, up to penny sized hail was observed.
episodes.174257: A slow-moving upper trough produced multiple rounds of thunderstorms over Labor Day weekend. Some of these storms produced damaging microbursts and severe hail.
episodes.174320: A weak push of monsoon moisture plus ongoing record heat fueled scattered thunderstorms over Mohave County. A few produced severe weather and flash flooding.
episodes.174321: A weak push of monsoon moisture plus ongoing record heat fueled a few thunderstorms which produced flash flooding in Death Valley National Park.
episodes.174322: A weak push of monsoon moisture plus ongoing record heat fueled a few thunderstorms over southwest Nevada. One produced severe weather.
episodes.174374: A small area of heavy rain showers and thunderstorms repeatedly developed and moved over the same areas of Oconee County during the overnight and early morning hours of the 3rd. Rainfall totals of 4-7 inches resulted in flash flooding across the western half of the county.
episodes.174439: Scattered thunderstorms developed along a weak stationary front near the Chatham County coast. One storm became strong enough to produce strong wind gusts.
episodes.174499: A frontal boundary that stalled across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi on September 2nd, slowly lifted northward through the day on September 3rd. Abundant moisture in place south of the boundary provided enough lift for showers and thunderstorms to develop. The existence and slow movement of the front resulted in slow moving storms. This resulted in heavy rainfall and flash flooding over portions of Baton Rouge and New Orleans.
episodes.174515: Abundant tropical moisture was over the Coastal Bend on September 3rd. Scattered thunderstorms with very heavy rainfall produced flash flooding in Corpus Christi.
episodes.174516: Locally heavy rainfall over saturated grounds caused flooding along Petronila and Oso creeks in southern Nueces County.
episodes.174545: Isolated gale-force wind gusts occurred in association with a convective shower moving northwest outside the Northwest Channel, about 14 miles northwest of Key West.
episodes.174573: Another weak mid-level shortwave trough pushed through the CWA, similar to the day before. Ample DCAPE values up to 1000 J/kg helped produce isolated thunderstorms across west central Kansas along or near the Hwy 83 corridor. Shear values were relatively weak but lapse rates were more marginal allowing for some downburst winds to perpetrate across this area of the CWA.
episodes.174948: The Snow Glacial Dam Release occurred around September 3rd 2022.  Partners had received a Glacial Dam Release reminder since Snow Glacial Dam Release occurs biannually and the previous release had been in 2020.  The initial release raised water levels on the Snow River which continued downstream to the Kenai River and on to Skilak Lake.  The capacity of Skilak Lake was large enough to absorb the Glacier Dammed Lake and prevent high water from traveling further downstream, producing only minor rises.

Wickenburg Police Department reported Vulture Mine Road at Sols Wash was closed due to flooding. The road was reported closed at 2005MST, but flooding impacts likely began around 1950MST based on radar and an upstream streamflow gage. The streamflow gage is roughly 2 miles upstream and measured 1.69 inches in 1 hour ending at 1900MST. Streamflow exceeded alarm stage at 1930MST. The gage peaked at 4.10 feet and 4815 cfs at 2010MST. Flow fell back below alarm stage at 2100MST.  No damages or injuries were reported.

A Facebook report showed flooding at the Brookwood Apartments in Columbia on West 7th Street and Academy Lane with several cars flooded. Damages are estimated for the flooded cars.

Multiple sources reported flash flooding developed over western Oconee County after 4 to 7 inches of rain fell in around 6 hours. Impacts were generally limited to inundated roads, including Stribling Shoals Rd and Coffee Rd at the confluence of White Fork and Coneross Creeks. The Chauga River and Ramsey Creek caused significant flooding of Chau Ram Park and Ramsey Creek Rd. Multiple roads were reported flooded and closed closer to Westminster, including Clearmont Rd, which was inundated by Colonels Fork Creek.
Although heavy rain tapered off across Oconee County during the late morning, flooding due to the overnight and early morning rainfall persisted into the early afternoon before receding.
High water was reported on several roads near the downtown area. Barricades were requested to close off affected roads.

Heavy rainfall resulted in flooding at the intersection of Corporate Boulevard and Energy Drive with water approximately 1 foot deep.

Heavy rain resulted in flash flooding in the Big Bend National Park. A section of the Lost Mine Trail collapsed which resulted in heavy damage to that section of trail. The bottom of the trail was covered in rocks and the top of the trail was too narrow to safely cross. The trail was closed as a result. Also, high water and debris crossed the pavement along the Ross Maxwell Scenic Drive. The pavement was broken off and washed away. Logs and rocks were washed onto the road which made it unsafe to travel. The damage and debris resulted in the road being closed. The cost of damage is a very rough estimate.
State Highway 286 between Farm to Market Roads 2444 and 70 was closed due to flooding.
Trees were reported down on Gold City Road near Franklin.

Eight to 10 inches of rain over a few hour period caused significant flash flooding over portions of western Switzerland County. Numerous creeks and streams were out of their banks. The hardest hit areas were in the vicinity of Bennington and along Indian Creek, where several county bridges were heavily damaged and a couple of bridges were washed out. Significant damage occurred to numerous homes along Indian Creek with trees also downed by the flowing water and roadways along the creek washed out in places.
Trees were blown over in the Weather Stone subdivision, which also brought down power lines.
Trees were blown down along Windsor Circle, which also brought down power lines.

A 64 year old woman was killed when water left the banks of Brushy Fork and swept away her house on Brushy Fork Road. A barn and all the family's belongings were also swept away in the flood waters. The body of the woman was found 5 miles downstream by family members after first responders suspended their efforts overnight. The value of the damaged property is unknown.

Widespread street flooding occurred in the Evansville metro area. The water was waist deep in spots. Some water rescues were conducted from stranded vehicles. In the large retail area on the east side of Evansville, Green River Road was flooded both north and south of the Lloyd Expressway. Flash flooding was reported all along Highway 41 in Evansville. The storm total rainfall was about three inches at rain gages in the county.

Storm total rainfall ranged up to 5.48 inches at a rain gage on the west side of Owensboro, near the east end of the Audubon Parkway where it meets Highway 60. A residential neighborhood in the immediate vicinity of this gage was flooded. There was also a report of 5.37 inches a mile west of the Owensboro airport.
